page: Microsoft Azure E64s_v5 is an ESv5-family virtual machine configured with 64 vCPUs and 512.0 GB of RAM, yielding an 8.0 GB memory-to-core ratio. Powered by an Intel Xeon 8370C processor operating at 2.8 GHz, this x86_64 architecture server features 32 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. The CPU allocation is fully dedicated, supported by a cache hierarchy of 48 KB L1d, 1 MB L2, and 48 MB L3 cache. It lacks local storage and GPUs, relying instead on external Premium Storage options.

Benchmark data indicates strong multi-core performance, with a stress-ng multi-core score of 62,152.98 and a Geekbench multi-core score of 16,533.0. Large-block memory bandwidth is highly efficient, reaching 296.85 GB/sec for read-only operations and 136.92 GB/sec for write operations. Single-core performance remains moderate, as evidenced by a Geekbench single-core score of 1,674.0 and a stress-ng single-core score of 1,899.89. The system excels in multi-threaded decompression and software compilation, but exhibits a clear bottleneck in large-scale LLM text generation, dropping to 2.73 tokens/sec on a 70B model.

Given its high memory density of 8 GB per vCPU and dedicated compute resources, the E64s_v5 offers a cost-efficient profile for memory-intensive enterprise workloads without the overhead of local NVMe drives. It is highly suited for large-scale database operations, high-throughput static web serving, and memory-bound multi-threaded applications. However, the lack of local storage requires external disk provisioning, and the absence of GPU acceleration makes it unsuitable for heavy deep learning training or real-time large language model inference.
description: The Microsoft Azure E64s_v5 is a memory-optimized virtual machine from the ESv5 family, featuring 64 dedicated vCPUs and 512.0 GB of RAM. Powered by an Intel Xeon 8370C processor running at 2.8 GHz, this x86_64 server delivers strong multi-core performance, as demonstrated by a multi-core Geekbench score of 16,533.0 and a Passmark CPU score of 60,927.22. While it lacks local storage and GPU hardware, it provides high memory bandwidth, reaching 296.85 GB/sec for large-block reads. Tradeoffs include average single-core speeds and weak performance in large-scale LLM text generation. This configuration is highly efficient for memory-intensive enterprise applications, database operations, and multi-threaded software compilation.
